summaryEn: Taiwan's solar industry collapse, contained in one company: revenue down 60%, a NT$6.24 per-share loss, and NT$395m of cash left. The plant has been rebuilt for N-type cells and the government is drafting new demand — but the shares trade at 3.7 times a book value that is shrinking fast.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + company earnings call; solar-collapse framing — the verified causes (frozen Taiwan market, change of government, sector stigmatisation), the 2025Q3 line shutdown and TOPCon rebuild, and the 2026 rooftop-replacement policy all credited, but the 2025Q4 loss of NT$2.22bn is flagged as far exceeding the nine-month loss discussed at the December call with its composition explicitly NOT verified and NOT asserted; NT$395m of cash against a NT$3.18bn trailing loss stated plainly; and the widely circulated claim linking the company to SpaceX is REJECTED — the company's own call places satellite cells at collaborative-development stage and names no customer; sector Optoelectronics → Solar Cells & Modules; meaningless P/E 0.00 stripped)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
TSEC (元晶太陽能, TWSE: 6443) makes solar cells and modules, and its accounts are the most severe in this collection. Founded in **2010** and **listed in October 2015**, it is one of Taiwan's largest domestic solar manufacturers — in a year when Taiwan's solar market effectively stopped. **FY2025 revenue fell 59.56%** and the company lost **NT$6.24 per share**. Trailing return on equity is **−89.77%**. It has **paid no dividend since FY2023**.

The causes are specific and verified from the company's own December 2025 earnings call: **the Taiwan market froze, a change of government interrupted policy continuity, and the solar sector was partly stigmatised** in public debate over ground-mounted installations. Taiwan installed only **818 MW in the first nine months of 2025**, against a previous run-rate above **2 GW**. On top of that, TSEC used the downturn to **shut its production lines in 2025Q3 and rebuild the cell plant** — raising capacity **25%** and converting fully to **TOPCon N-type technology**, with cell and module plants now running two lines each at **1 GW** — absorbing depreciation, demolition costs, trial-production scrap and one-off severance while producing almost nothing.

**One figure could not be verified and is presented as such.** At that December call, management discussed a nine-month net loss of **NT$976m**. The full year came in at **−NT$6.24 per share**, meaning **the fourth quarter alone lost NT$2.22bn** — more than double the first nine months combined — with a **gross margin of −217.5%** and an **operating margin of −563.2%**. Figures of that shape normally indicate write-downs rather than ordinary trading, but **the composition of that charge could not be independently confirmed, and no explanation is asserted here.**

**One widely circulated claim is rejected outright.** Headlines describing TSEC as a supplier to Elon Musk's SpaceX are **not supported by the company's own disclosure**. Its earnings call places satellite solar cells at **collaborative development stage — not production** — states that satellite manufacturers have approached it, notes the attraction of a market with a **15–20% annual replacement rate**, and **names no customer and does not mention SpaceX**. That is the whole of what the company has said, and it is all this page will say.

The financial position is tight. **Cash of NT$395m** against **equity of NT$3.54bn**, **NT$6.35bn of assets**, a **44.2% debt ratio**, and **2026Q1 operating cash flow of −NT$96m**. Yet the shares trade at **NT$25.60 — 3.70× book** — meaning the market is valuing something other than the solar business. The reported P/E of 0.00× has been removed from this page as meaningless on a loss-making basis.

There are genuine positives: **2026Q1's loss narrowed sharply to NT$0.20 per share**, the plant is now N-type, government policy on **rooftop replacement could create 1.3–1.4 GW of potential demand** with new subsidies adding around **400 MW**, and management targets **cell sales above 550 MW and module sales above 500 MW** in 2026. The honest read: **a rebuilt factory waiting for a policy-driven market to return, with a shrinking equity base, very little cash, and a share price disconnected from both.**

TSEC was founded in **2010**, near the peak of global optimism about solar manufacturing. Taiwan had built a substantial position in **solar cells** — the wafer-based devices that convert light to electricity — supplying them to module assemblers worldwide. The industrial logic was familiar: Taiwan was already excellent at semiconductor-adjacent processing, and solar cells are made with similar equipment and discipline. The company **listed in October 2015**.

What happened next to the whole industry is well documented. **China built solar manufacturing capacity at a scale no other country could match**, supported by policy and finance, and drove module prices down by an order of magnitude. That was extraordinary for the world's energy transition and ruinous for everyone else's manufacturers. Taiwanese solar companies consolidated, exited, or retreated to the **domestic market**, where local content and energy-security considerations offered some shelter.

TSEC took the domestic route, becoming one of Taiwan's largest local cell and module makers, serving an installation market underpinned by government renewable-energy targets. That worked while the targets were being pursued. Then, in 2025, three things happened at once: **the Taiwan market froze**, a **change of government** disrupted policy continuity, and **the solar sector was partly stigmatised** in public controversy over ground-mounted installations and land use. Installations fell to **818 MW in the first nine months of 2025**, against a previous rate above **2 GW**.

Facing a market that had simply stopped buying, management made a decision that was defensible and expensive: **shut the lines in the third quarter and rebuild the factory**. Capacity rose **25%**, the plant converted fully to **TOPCon N-type cells** — the current mainstream high-efficiency technology — and the company absorbed depreciation on idle assets, demolition costs, trial-production scrap and redundancy payments while producing almost nothing. It is the choice of a company betting that the market returns. Whether it can afford the wait is now the question, with **NT$395m of cash** on the balance sheet.

- **2010 (24 June)** — TSEC founded to manufacture solar cells.
- **2015 (1 Oct)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (6443)**.
- **2010s** — Chinese capacity expansion collapses global module prices; TSEC concentrates on Taiwan's domestic installation market.
- **2022** — **FY2022 EPS NT$0.41**; dividend **NT$0.1**.
- **2023** — Best recent year: **FY2023 EPS NT$1.08**; dividend **NT$0.4** — the last dividend paid.
- **2024** — Deterioration begins; **FY2024 EPS −NT$1.17**, with **Q4 alone at −NT$1.31**.
- **2025** — **The collapse.** Taiwan's market freezes amid a change of government and public controversy over solar installations; installations reach only **818 MW in nine months** against a previous rate above 2 GW. **FY2025 revenue −59.56%; FY2025 EPS −NT$6.24.**
- **2025Q3** — **Production lines shut with almost no output** while the cell plant is rebuilt: capacity **+25%**, full conversion to **TOPCon N-type**; costs absorbed include depreciation, demolition, trial-production scrap and one-off severance. Q3 EPS **−NT$1.21**.
- **2025 (5 Dec)** — Earnings call discusses a **nine-month net loss of NT$976m** and frames 2025 as the trough; guides recovery in **2026Q2 or Q3**; describes satellite cells as at **collaborative development stage**, naming no customer.
- **2025Q4** — **A loss of NT$2.22bn (EPS −NT$4.34)** — more than double the first nine months — with **gross margin −217.5%** and **operating margin −563.2%**. *(Composition not independently verified.)*
- **2026Q1** — Loss narrows sharply to **−NT$0.20 per share**; cell and module plants now **two TOPCon N-type lines each at 1 GW**; 2026 targets of **cells >550 MW, modules >500 MW**.

TSEC's accounts describe **a company that spent its worst year rebuilding its factory, and has limited resources left to wait for the market**.

- **The scale of the loss.** **FY2025 revenue fell 59.56%** and the company lost **NT$6.24 per share**. The annual series reads **NT$0.41 (FY2022) → 1.08 (FY2023) → −1.17 (FY2024) → −NT$6.24 (FY2025)**. Trailing **return on equity is −89.77%** — the company lost close to the equivalent of nine-tenths of its equity over twelve months.
- **The fourth quarter, and what is not known about it.** At the **5 December 2025** earnings call, management discussed a **nine-month net loss of NT$976m**. The full year implies **2025Q4 alone lost NT$2.22bn**, with a **gross margin of −217.5%** and an **operating margin of −563.2%** — costs several times revenue. Ratios of that magnitude are typically produced by **write-downs rather than trading losses**, but **the composition of the charge could not be independently verified**, and this page does not assert one. Readers should consult the company's own filings.
- **The 2025Q3 rebuild was deliberate and costly.** With the market frozen, TSEC **shut its lines and reconstructed the cell plant**: capacity **+25%**, full conversion to **TOPCon N-type**, and cell and module plants each now running **two lines at 1 GW**. The quarter absorbed **depreciation on idle assets, demolition costs, trial-production scrap and one-off severance**.
- **Liquidity is the binding constraint.** **NT$395m of cash** against **NT$3.54bn of equity** and **NT$6.35bn of assets**, with a **44.2% debt ratio** and **2026Q1 operating cash flow of −NT$96m**. That is a thin buffer for a company that lost **NT$3.18bn** over the trailing twelve months, even with losses now narrowing sharply.
- **No dividend since FY2023.** The record shows only **NT$0.1 (FY2022)** and **NT$0.4 (FY2023)**. **Dividend yield is 0.00%**, accurately.
- **The valuation does not reflect the accounts.** At **NT$25.60 the shares trade at 3.70× book** — a substantial premium to an equity base that the last twelve months reduced sharply. Whatever the market is pricing, it is not the current solar business. The reported **P/E of 0.00× has been removed** from this page as meaningless on a loss-making basis.
- **The turn has begun.** **2026Q1's loss narrowed to NT$0.20 per share** from **NT$4.34** in the prior quarter, with gross margin improving from **−217.5% to −5.1%** — still negative, but a different order of magnitude.

The financing reality: **a rebuilt, technically current factory attached to a balance sheet with very little margin for another bad year.**

**Stance: a rebuilt N-type solar plant waiting for a policy-driven domestic market to restart — with NT$395m of cash, a 90% negative return on equity, and a share price at 3.7 times a shrinking book value.**

The case for:

1. **The factory is now technically current.** The 2025Q3 rebuild converted the plant **fully to TOPCon N-type** — the mainstream high-efficiency technology — and **raised capacity 25%**, with cell and module plants each running **two lines at 1 GW**. The cost has been taken; the capability is in place.
2. **Policy could restore the market.** Government measures on **rooftop replacement** are estimated to create **1.3–1.4 GW of potential demand**, with new subsidies adding around **400 MW**. Management expects demand to recover in **2026Q2 or Q3** and targets **cell sales above 550 MW and module sales above 500 MW**.
3. **The loss is narrowing fast.** From **−NT$4.34 per share in 2025Q4 to −NT$0.20 in 2026Q1**, with gross margin improving from **−217.5% to −5.1%**.
4. **Domestic positioning has strategic value.** Taiwan's energy security argues for local solar manufacturing that does not depend on Chinese supply — the same logic the company cites for its interest in satellite cells, a market it says lets it avoid unfair Chinese competition.

The case against:

- **Liquidity.** **NT$395m of cash** against a **trailing loss of NT$3.18bn** and **negative operating cash flow**. This is the risk that overrides every other consideration.
- **An unexplained fourth-quarter charge.** **NT$2.22bn lost in 2025Q4** — more than double the nine months discussed at the December call — with a **−563.2% operating margin**. Its composition is not verified.
- **Demand depends on government decisions**, in a sector that has become politically contentious in Taiwan.
- **The valuation.** **3.70× book** for a business that has just destroyed a large part of that book, with **no dividend since FY2023**.
- **The satellite story is not a business yet.** The company describes it as **collaborative development**, names **no customer**, and has **not mentioned SpaceX** — despite headlines that say otherwise.

A **speculative recovery** thesis: everything depends on Taiwanese installations returning before the cash runs out.

TSEC manufactures the two physical products at the heart of a solar installation:

- **Solar cells.** Silicon wafers processed into devices that convert sunlight into electricity. This is semiconductor-adjacent manufacturing — deposition, diffusion, patterning, metallisation — and cell **efficiency** is the competitive variable. The plant has now been **fully converted to TOPCon N-type**, the current mainstream high-efficiency architecture, with **two lines totalling 1 GW**.
- **Modules.** Cells assembled into laminated, framed panels with glass, encapsulant and backsheet — the finished product installed on roofs and land. Module capacity is likewise **two lines at 1 GW**.
- **How the money is made, and why it stopped.** Revenue is **megawatts shipped times price per watt**; profit is that price minus manufacturing cost. Because module prices are set globally by Chinese oversupply and manufacturing cost is largely **fixed capacity being depreciated**, profitability depends almost entirely on **utilisation**. When Taiwan's installations fell to **818 MW in nine months** from a rate above **2 GW**, utilisation collapsed and fixed costs remained — which is how a company reaches a **−217.5% gross margin**.
- **Why the domestic market matters so much.** TSEC cannot compete on cost with Chinese producers in export markets. Its business exists because Taiwan installs solar domestically, with local supply preferred for energy-security and policy reasons. That makes **government renewable-energy policy the company's demand curve**, which is both its protection and its dependence.
- **The satellite ambition, stated exactly as the company states it.** TSEC has said satellite manufacturers "in the global democratic camp" have approached it about **jointly developing cells and modules for satellites**, that the market has a **15–20% annual replacement rate**, and that it offers a way to avoid unfair Chinese competition. The company describes this as a **medium-to-long-term strategy at collaborative development stage** — **not production** — and has **named no customer**.

The levers are **Taiwanese installation volumes, capacity utilisation, cell efficiency and module pricing**. The strength is a rebuilt, current-technology plant with domestic-supply positioning. The vulnerability is total: **a fixed-cost manufacturer whose demand is set by government policy, with NT$395m of cash to wait with.**

Solar manufacturing is the clearest case anywhere of a technology succeeding so completely that its manufacturers stopped making money.

- **What China did.** Chinese producers built solar manufacturing capacity at a scale no other country approached, backed by policy and finance, and drove module prices down by an order of magnitude over roughly fifteen years. This has been an enormous benefit to global decarbonisation and a catastrophe for non-Chinese manufacturers, most of whom exited. **Chinese producers themselves have been operating at a loss**, which does nothing to relieve the pressure — loss-making capacity still produces.
- **Why national solar industries persist anyway.** Countries maintain domestic solar manufacturing for **energy security and supply-chain resilience**, not cost. That creates protected domestic demand — and makes those manufacturers dependent on the policies that create it.
- **Taiwan's particular problem.** Taiwan's solar deployment relies heavily on land, and **ground-mounted installations became politically contentious** — over farmland use, fish ponds and permitting. Combined with a **change of government** and the resulting policy discontinuity, installations fell to **818 MW in the first nine months of 2025** from a rate above **2 GW**. This was not a technology failure or a competitive loss; **the domestic customer simply stopped buying**.
- **The technology transition.** The industry moved from PERC to **N-type TOPCon** cells for higher efficiency. Manufacturers who did not convert became uncompetitive; TSEC converted, at the cost of a shut quarter.
- **What could restart it.** Taiwan's policy direction has shifted toward **rooftop rather than ground-mounted** solar, which avoids the land controversy. Estimates put the **rooftop-replacement opportunity at 1.3–1.4 GW**, with new subsidies adding around **400 MW**.

TSEC's position is **entirely dependent on Taiwan's policy choices**. The industry truth is that **a domestic solar manufacturer is a policy instrument with a share price** — protected from Chinese competition by local preference, and exposed to the political weather in a way no ordinary manufacturer is.

**Strengths**
- **Rebuilt, technically current plant**: full conversion to **TOPCon N-type**, capacity **+25%**, cell and module plants each **two lines at 1 GW**.
- **Domestic positioning** in a market that prefers local supply for energy-security reasons.
- **Loss narrowing sharply**: **−NT$4.34 (2025Q4) → −NT$0.20 (2026Q1)**; gross margin **−217.5% → −5.1%**.

**Weaknesses**
- **NT$395m of cash** against a trailing loss of **NT$3.18bn**; **2026Q1 operating cash flow −NT$96m**.
- **FY2025 revenue −59.56%, EPS −NT$6.24, trailing ROE −89.77%.**
- **A NT$2.22bn fourth-quarter loss whose composition is not verifiable** from public sources.
- **No dividend since FY2023**; shares at **3.70× a shrinking book value**.

**Opportunities**
- **Rooftop-replacement policy**: estimated **1.3–1.4 GW** potential demand, plus around **400 MW** from new subsidies.
- Management targets **cells >550 MW and modules >500 MW** in 2026, with recovery expected in Q2 or Q3.
- **Satellite cells** — at collaborative development stage, in a market with a **15–20% annual replacement rate**.

**Threats**
- **Further policy delay** in a politically contentious sector.
- **Liquidity** — limited capacity to absorb another weak year without raising capital.
- Continued Chinese oversupply capping module pricing globally.

- **Liquidity is the overriding risk.** **NT$395m of cash** against **NT$3.54bn of equity**, a **trailing twelve-month loss of NT$3.18bn**, and **negative operating cash flow in 2026Q1**. Losses have narrowed dramatically, which helps — but the buffer for another weak year is small, and any recapitalisation would dilute existing shareholders substantially.
- **A large fourth-quarter charge that cannot be explained from public sources.** **2025Q4 lost NT$2.22bn** — more than double the **NT$976m** nine-month loss management discussed on **5 December 2025** — with a **−217.5% gross margin** and **−563.2% operating margin**. Ratios of that shape usually indicate write-downs, but **this page does not assert a composition it could not verify**. Anyone evaluating the company should read the annual filing directly.
- **Demand is a government decision.** Taiwan's installations fell to **818 MW in nine months** because of a frozen market, a change of administration and public controversy over solar land use. The **rooftop-replacement policy** may restore demand — but the timing, scale and durability are political, not commercial.
- **The valuation is disconnected from the accounts.** **3.70× book** for a company whose book value the last year materially reduced, with **no earnings and no dividend**.
- **Claims circulating about satellite customers are not supported by company disclosure.** TSEC describes satellite cells as **collaborative development, not production**, and has **named no customer and not mentioned SpaceX**. Investors relying on headlines to the contrary are relying on something the company has not said.
- **Structural cost disadvantage.** Even with a rebuilt N-type plant, TSEC cannot match Chinese scale on cost. Its business depends on domestic preference persisting.

TSEC's outlook is a straightforward race: **does Taiwan's solar market restart before the balance sheet runs out of room?** The axes to watch:

- **Cash and operating cash flow.** The variable that determines whether anything else matters. **NT$395m of cash** and **−NT$96m of operating cash flow in 2026Q1**. Any announcement of a capital raise would be the most important news the company could produce.
- **Taiwanese installation volumes.** The demand curve. Installations of **818 MW in nine months of 2025** against a prior rate above **2 GW**; the **rooftop-replacement policy** is estimated at **1.3–1.4 GW** of potential demand with about **400 MW** more from new subsidies. Management expects recovery in **2026Q2 or Q3**.
- **Utilisation against the 2026 targets.** **Cells above 550 MW and modules above 500 MW**, against installed capacity of **1 GW each**. Because costs are fixed, utilisation is the whole of the margin story — which is why gross margin swung from **−217.5% to −5.1%** in one quarter.
- **Quarterly losses continuing to narrow.** **−NT$4.34 → −NT$0.20** is the right direction; reaching break-even is the milestone that would change the situation.
- **The satellite programme.** Currently **collaborative development with no named customer**. Any move to actual orders or production would be genuinely new information — and should be judged against company disclosure, not headlines.

Bottom line: TSEC took Taiwan's solar collapse full in the face — **revenue down 59.56%, a NT$6.24 per-share loss, ROE of −89.77%** — and used the worst of it to **rebuild its factory to TOPCon N-type with 25% more capacity**, betting that a policy-driven domestic market returns. Losses have narrowed sharply to **−NT$0.20 per share**, and the rooftop-replacement policy could restore demand. But it holds **NT$395m of cash**, carries an **unexplained NT$2.22bn fourth-quarter charge**, pays no dividend, and trades at **3.70× a book value that has just shrunk**. Judge it on **cash, Taiwanese installation volumes and utilisation** — a rebuilt factory waiting on a political decision.
